questions.stem: Which feature is shared by every eukaryotic organism?

options.text: Their DNA sits inside a nucleus enclosed by its own membrane
options.explanation: This is the universal eukaryotic signature named in the note.

options.text: Their cells always contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis
options.explanation: Fungi and animals never photosynthesise, so this cannot be universal.

options.text: They are always built from many cooperating cells
options.explanation: Yeasts and many protoctists live as single cells, so multicellularity is not shared.

options.text: Their genetic material floats freely in the cytoplasm
options.explanation: That describes prokaryotes, the group the note contrasts against eukaryotes.

questions.stem: Which list contains only eukaryotic groups?

options.text: Protoctists, animals, bacteria, plants
options.explanation: Again bacteria sneak in; the fourth slot should be fungi.

options.text: Animals, plants, fungi, protoctists
options.explanation: These are exactly the four eukaryote groups the note names.

options.text: Animals, plants, bacteria, fungi
options.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotic, so the list mixes the two camps.

options.text: Plants, fungi, protoctists, viruses
options.explanation: Viruses sit outside the classification of living organisms altogether.
options.misconception: viruses misfiled as a eukaryote group

questions.stem: A single-celled organism is found to have a membrane-enclosed nucleus. How should it be classified?

options.text: A virus, because it has so few parts
options.explanation: Viruses have no cellular structure at all, let alone a nucleus.
options.misconception: virus treated as a small cell

options.text: Neither group, because classification needs multicellularity
options.explanation: Nothing in the classification demands many cells.

options.text: A eukaryote, because body size does not change the cell plan
options.explanation: Single-celled eukaryotes exist, so the nucleus decides the group.

options.text: A prokaryote, because all single cells are prokaryotic
options.explanation: Plenty of protoctists and yeasts are single cells with enclosed nuclei.

questions.stem: Under a light microscope, which observation most directly supports calling a cell eukaryotic?

options.text: The cell has a regular rectangular outline
options.explanation: Shape tells you about the wall, not about DNA packaging.
options.misconception: cell shape used as nuclear evidence

options.text: The specimen moves across the field of view
options.explanation: Movement is a life process, not a cell-plan feature.

options.text: The cell stains darker at its edges than at its centre
options.explanation: Edge staining says nothing reliable about the nucleus.

options.text: A dark rounded region enclosed by a distinct membrane is visible
options.explanation: That is the nucleus, the deciding eukaryotic feature.

questions.stem: Why can body design never settle whether an organism is eukaryotic?

options.text: Because eukaryotes and prokaryotes each include both single-celled and many-celled members
options.explanation: The note states eukaryotes may be single-celled or multicellular, so body design cuts across both camps.

options.text: Because every living thing is made of exactly one cell
options.explanation: Animals and plants are obviously many-celled.

options.text: Because only organisms with cell walls can be many-celled
options.explanation: Animal cells lack walls yet build whole bodies.

options.text: Because microscopes cannot resolve whether a body has one cell
options.explanation: Cell count is exactly what microscopy resolves well.

questions.stem: State the shared cell feature that defines the eukaryote camp.
questions.modelAnswer: A nucleus that holds the DNA and is enclosed by its own membrane.

questions.stem: Name the four eukaryotic groups covered by this course.
A classmate sorts organisms into 'single-celled' versus 'many-celled' and calls the first pile prokaryotes. Explain the flaw in that sorting.
questions.modelAnswer: The piles confuse body design with cell plan: several protoctists and the yeast fungus are single cells yet carry an enclosed nucleus, which makes them eukaryotes, while some prokaryotes can cling together in clumps without becoming many-celled organisms.

questions.stem: A pond sample yields an organism that is one cell, about twice the length of a bacterium, and clearly shows a rounded structure enclosed by a double membrane. Which camp does it belong to, and what additional observation would tell you which of the four groups it sits in?
questions.modelAnswer: It is a eukaryote because its genetic material sits in a membrane-enclosed nucleus; grouping it further needs observations such as chloroplasts (plant-like), a chitin-based hyphal or yeast form (fungus), feeding by ingesting or absorbing, or none of those (protoctist).

questions.stem: Which combination correctly lists a plant-only feature and an animal-only feature?

options.text: Nucleus with its own membrane — starch store
options.explanation: The enclosed nucleus is common to both groups; starch belongs to plants.

options.text: Cellulose cell wall — glycogen carbohydrate store
options.explanation: Walls with cellulose belong to plants; glycogen storage belongs to animals.

options.text: Chloroplasts — cellulose cell wall
options.explanation: Both features sit on the plant side of the comparison.
options.misconception: two plant traits labelled as the animal pair

options.text: Glycogen store — mitochondria present
options.explanation: Mitochondria appear in both groups, so they cannot separate them.

questions.stem: A stained slide shows cells with visible chloroplasts and a thin outer wall. Which group do they come from?

options.text: Fungi
options.explanation: Fungal walls are not built with cellulose and the group has no chloroplasts.

options.text: Protoctists
options.explanation: Some protoctists photosynthesise, but the combination with a cellulose wall matches the plant list here.

options.text: Plants
options.explanation: Chloroplasts plus a wall is the classic plant-cell pairing.

options.text: Animals
options.explanation: Animal cells never carry chloroplasts or walls.

questions.stem: Which statement about carbohydrate storage is correct for these two groups?

options.text: Plants bank glycogen; animals bank starch
options.explanation: The two stores have been swapped.

options.text: Both groups bank starch
options.explanation: Animal cells store carbohydrate as glycogen instead.

options.text: Neither group stores carbohydrate
options.explanation: Both groups maintain a carbohydrate reserve.

options.text: Plants bank starch; animals bank glycogen
options.explanation: The note names starch for plants and glycogen for animals.

questions.stem: What do animal cells and plant cells BOTH possess?

options.text: A nucleus enclosed by its own membrane and mitochondria
options.explanation: Both groups run the core eukaryotic plan including mitochondria.

options.text: A cellulose wall and chloroplasts
options.explanation: Those belong to plant cells only.

options.text: Chloroplasts but no mitochondria
options.explanation: Plant cells contain mitochondria alongside their chloroplasts.

options.text: A cellulose wall but no nucleus
options.explanation: Both groups are eukaryotic, so nuclei are present in both.

questions.stem: Why is the absence of a cell wall a reliable marker for animal cells in this course?

options.text: Because walls appear only in single-celled organisms
options.explanation: Plant bodies are many-celled with walls on every cell.

options.text: Because plant cells carry a cellulose wall and fungal cells are walled too, while animal cells run without one
options.explanation: The wall contrast separates animal cells from both other many-celled groups.

options.text: Because animal cells are always spherical
options.explanation: Shape varies across animal tissues.

options.text: Because animal cells cannot survive with a wall
options.explanation: The note never claims walls harm animal cells.

questions.stem: List three structures an animal cell has that the note names, besides the nucleus.
State the material that plant cell walls are built from and the plant carbohydrate store.
questions.modelAnswer: Walls are built from cellulose, and the store is starch.

questions.stem: Explain why chloroplasts let plants count as self-feeders while animals must find food.
questions.modelAnswer: Chloroplasts capture light energy and drive photosynthesis, so a plant can manufacture the sugars it needs from simple raw materials, whereas animal cells carry no chloroplasts and must take in ready-made organic food.

questions.stem: A food label lists a carbohydrate reserve harvested from an unknown organism. Chemical tests show the reserve is glycogen. Which of the two groups did the organism belong to, and which organelle would you expect its cells to contain for releasing energy from that reserve?
questions.modelAnswer: Glycogen points to the animal group, since plants bank starch; its cells would contain mitochondria to release energy from the stored carbohydrate.

questions.stem: Which structure builds the bodies of multicellular fungi?

options.text: Muscle and nerve tissues
options.explanation: Those are animal tissues.

options.text: Free-floating colonies of identical single cells only
options.explanation: Multicellular fungi are hyphal, not loose cell colonies.

options.text: Thread-like hyphae containing many nuclei
options.explanation: The note describes hyphae as the thread-like building units of multicellular fungi.

options.text: Cellulose leaves and stems
options.explanation: That is plant anatomy.

questions.stem: Which fungus is named as the single-celled example?

options.text: Mucor
options.explanation: Mucor is the named multicellular genus.

options.text: Lactobacillus
options.explanation: That is a bacterium, not a fungus.

options.text: Plasmodium
options.explanation: That is a protoctist.

options.text: Yeast
options.explanation: The note names yeast as the single-celled fungus.

questions.stem: Why does the protoctist group resist a one-line definition?

options.text: Because its members are too varied to share one distinguishing trait beyond the eukaryotic plan
options.explanation: The note calls the group very diverse with features differing from the other three groups.

options.text: Because all protoctists are photosynthetic
options.explanation: Only some are; the group is not uniform.

options.text: Because they have no nuclei
options.explanation: Protoctists are eukaryotes with enclosed nuclei.

options.text: Because they are all parasitic
options.explanation: The note gives no such blanket claim.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a cell with a wall, an enclosed nucleus, mitochondria and no chloroplasts, growing as a thread of connected compartments. Best match?

options.text: An animal skin cell
options.explanation: Animal cells have neither walls nor hyphal threading.

options.text: A fungal cell from a hypha
options.explanation: Wall plus enclosed nucleus, mitochondria, no chloroplasts, hyphal thread — the fungal portrait.

options.text: A plant leaf cell
options.explanation: Leaf cells carry chloroplasts.

options.text: A bacterial cell
options.explanation: Bacteria lack the enclosed nucleus.

questions.stem: Which exam skill does the note explicitly flag for fungi and protoctists?

options.text: Calculating their surface-area-to-volume ratios
options.explanation: That belongs to transport notes, not this one.

options.text: Staining them with iodine to test for starch
options.explanation: Iodine testing is a food-test technique, not a classification skill.

options.text: Recognising, drawing and labelling their cells from images
options.explanation: The closing hint names practising labelled drawings of fungal and protoctist cells.

options.text: Measuring their generation times in culture
options.explanation: No growth-rate work appears in this note.

questions.stem: Give the word for the thread-like filaments that build multicellular fungi.
questions.modelAnswer: Hyphae — thread-like filaments packed with nuclei.

questions.stem: Name one single-celled fungus and one disease-causing protoctist mentioned across this topic.
questions.modelAnswer: Yeast is the single-celled fungus; Plasmodium is the malaria protoctist.

questions.stem: Explain why a yeast cell counts as a fungus rather than as a protoctist.
questions.modelAnswer: Yeast carries the fungal toolkit — a wall, an enclosed nucleus and no chloroplasts — and it reproduces and feeds the fungal way, so it is placed with fungi even though it lives as a single cell; protoctists are identified only after the three defined groups have been ruled out.

questions.stem: A new microscope sample shows a many-celled organism built from branching threads with walls, several nuclei per compartment and no chloroplasts. Assign it to a group and justify the assignment with two features.
questions.modelAnswer: It belongs with the fungi: the branching thread construction matches hyphae, and the combination of walls with no chloroplasts plus many nuclei per compartment is the fungal portrait rather than the plant one.
